Seems to me like requiring "your password must contain an uppercase and lowercase letter, special character, number, be at least 8 characters long, and must be changed every 4 months" just causes people to keep a "password.txt" on their desktop which is arguably worse than someone just setting their password to "hello" and never changing it (brute force and dictionary attacks can be made more difficult if the service blocks excessive login attempts). I often see things that nobody is likely to break into set a very strong password policy. Apparently my college homework needed to be more secure than my bank account. My school had a password policy exactly like the one I described while I was there but my bank account basically has no password policy at all. I could see needing more security to protect my money but for something like schoolwork I'd rather have convenience over security.

Yes I know you could encrypt your password file or use a password manager and then make your passwords crazy strong but most average people aren't going to do this.
Can password policies do more harm than good?

That's why you use a password manager like Last Pass or KeePassX. Your passwords are encrypted and you only need your master password to open it. Which, if you have a finger print reader, you can use that so only you can unlock the password.

I addressed this in an edit I just made. Yes an encrypted password file or a password manager solves this problem somewhat but few people (especially non-techies) actually do this and with companies that have strong password rules may even be against company policy.
I would prefer going to full on sentences or several words mix with foreign ones. I hate when sites limit the length of your password.

I have 8 systems to log into each day for work, and they each have their own set of standards of how to create a password, and when to change it. All of my coworkers keep their passwords in a notebook of some kind at their desk. The password policy might protect from online intruders, but if someone broke into the building, with just a little digging they could access all of our systems.
Simply use a pass phrase easy to remember and nearly impossible to break into without company involvement.
